summary: A 1980 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols. It replaced RFC 758 and was replaced by RFC 770. It is historic.

eli5.summary: A big list saying which number means which thing in the network's rules. It was later replaced by a newer list.

subtitle: The assigned-numbers registry for internet protocols in January 1980

tldr.problem: Network and internet protocols were expanding; the 1979 assigned-numbers registry needed updates for new services, more network nodes, and protocol variants.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel released RFC 762 listing all then-current assignments: link and port numbers, network identifiers (now 34 assigned), protocol versions, internet protocol numbers, and socket numbers. New entries included MITRE Cablenet, AUTODIN II, COMSAT Distributed Computing Network, and various NIFTP variants.
tldr.outcome: The registry continued to serve as the authoritative source. It was soon replaced by RFC 770, establishing a pattern of regular updates.

today: RFC 762 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 770. These periodic registries evolved into the modern IANA system, which now maintains comprehensive, real-time registries for all internet protocols and address spaces.

sections.title: The 1980 Registry Update
sections.content:
RFC 762 is the 1980 update to the assigned numbers registry, published as Internet Experiment Note 127. Jon Postel continued to manage the registry, which now covered assigned port or socket numbers (serving both the AHHP and TCP), network identifiers, protocol versions, and protocol numbers.

This version consolidates ten earlier documents (RFCs 758, 755, 750, 739, 604, 503, 433, 349 and IENs 117, 93), reflecting the growing complexity of network protocols and the need for a single, authoritative source.
sections.eli5: The registry was updated once more, now with more networks and protocols added in the year since the last version.

sections.title: Expanded Assignments and New Services
sections.content:
Network numbers grew to 34 assigned (from 26 in RFC 755), including new entries: MITRE Cablenet (23), BBN Local Network (24), AUTODIN II (26), NOSC/LCCN (27), Wide Band Satellite Network (28), COMSAT DCN (29), UCL DCN (30), and Cambridge Rings (32–33). The port/socket section added new services: Name Server (42), WhoIs (43), Internet Message Processing Module (45), NI FTP (47), RAND Conference (49), and Simple Internet Mail (51).

Host-specific functions also expanded to include NIFTP variants at multiple sites (CADC, NPL, BNPL, Cambridge, Harwell, Swurcc, Essex, Rutherford). Protocol format identifiers now include raw internet datagrams, TCP variants, UDP (protocol 17), Multiplexing, and experimental protocols.
sections.eli5: Many more networks, services, and protocol types were added to the list. Different sites added special services with different numbers.

sections.title: Registry Governance
sections.content:
RFC 762 maintains the pattern of Jon Postel managing assignments. The RFC notes that current information was available from him, and anyone developing a protocol or application needing number assignments should contact USC-ISI.

RFC 762 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 770. These updates—approximately annual—eventually led to the formal establishment of IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) and the structured number assignment process used by the modern internet.
sections.eli5: Jon kept updating it as new things needed numbers. This kept happening every year or so, until eventually a more formal process took over.
